cells.tense: Right now you can hold several true things at once and still tell which is which.
cells.ask: Offer one thing you know before you're sure it fits, and let it be judged on what it does.
cells.core:
You can hold several true things at once and still tell which is which. That happens while you're talking, and it happens without you announcing it. It's the thing people around you are standing on, whether or not they've said so.
And the pen is in your hand. What you say about your own life is yours to state plainly, without checking first whether it's allowed. The balance here isn't stillness — it's the next thing you declare out loud about who you are and what you can do. Say it before you've finished rehearsing it. Then add the next one while that one is still landing, and let it be something you could actually get wrong.
cells.sheetLine: You can hold several things true at once. Keep stating your own.
cells.verb: holding many true things at once and telling which is which
cells.place: where what you are comes out as what you do

cells.tense: You're rehearsing what you'll say once the version of you ahead is finished.
cells.ask: Name one direction you're actually walking and drop the others for a week; let what you do be the argument.
cells.core:
You've got more true things in hand than any one life can use, and you're waiting for the version of you on the other side to pick among them. So picking keeps getting pushed forward — one more read, one more angle before you commit to anything.
That wait is costing you something real. What you're postponing isn't only decisions; it's what your life would look like if you stopped hedging. Pick one direction and stay in it for a week — not because it's the final answer, but because walking one path is how you find out what you're made of. The shine comes from something actually finished, not from one more version in rehearsal. Everything you're holding is still there when the week ends.
cells.sheetLine: You're saving your life for a version of you that hasn't started yet.

cells.tense: You saw what was true and you keep the door between yourself and saying it.
cells.ask: Tell one person the whole of one true thing — nothing hedged, nothing added after — and let it land.
cells.core:
What you saw is still in you. What isn't is the saying of it out loud. Somewhere it got easier to review the choices than to make one, and reviewing became the whole activity. You can describe the door exactly and not step through it.
But you don't need a new insight or a new year. Take one of the true things you've already seen and say it out loud to one person, whole, without softening it. Let it land while you're in the room. What they do with it isn't the point; saying it is what brings you back into the part of your life where you decide things instead of reviewing them.
cells.sheetLine: What you saw is still in you. Say it out loud to someone.

cells.tense: You keep saying you're still working it out while the answer is already sitting there decided.
cells.ask: Say out loud one conclusion you've already drawn, and keep the credit for having drawn it.
cells.core:
You've decided. More than once, you've come back to the same answer on some question that matters, and then described yourself as still working it out. The decision is real; the ownership is off. It's running as if it belonged to the situation rather than to you.
You know what's fair here, and you know which conclusion is already yours. So claim it in plain words to yourself first, then to someone who'll remember you said it, and keep the credit. That's what makes it yours in the living, not just in passing. You don't need a better answer — you mostly need to stop presenting a settled thing as undecided.
cells.sheetLine: You've already decided. Say it like it's yours.

attempts.check: The record does not support saying the person has stopped speaking their knowing out loud, or that a specific bad room taught them to hold back — so the Too Little cell locates the withholding as a present fact of the capacity and says nothing about its history or its cost. A reader could reasonably object that they are simply quiet, not withholding, so the cell names only what is observable (the keeping of it, the narration instead of the beginning) and lets them correct it. The ask survives being wrong: telling one true thing whole to one person — no hedging, nothing after it — is useful whether or not the read is right. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is 'You are becoming what you are,' which flatters and says nothing; it is not in any cell.
